issues.claim: Handlers are ordinary classes with no extra dependency on the library, so dropping it is a mechanical replacement, not a rewrite.
issues.problem: A MediatR handler must implement IRequestHandler<,>, so it does depend on the library interface. The rule is only accurate if "extra" is read as "beyond the handler interface", and a candidate could take it to mean no dependency at all.
issues.suggestedFix: Reword: "Keep handlers thin and put the business logic in plain classes or services, so that dropping the library only means rewriting the handler signatures and the registration." Apply the same change in the ru block.

issues.claim: Over time the mediator itself risks becoming a God object.
issues.problem: The fetched Refactoring.Guru excerpt is cut off before the pros and cons section, so it does not show this claim. I confirmed it from the page's cons list ('a mediator can evolve into a God Object') in my own knowledge, not from the excerpt.
issues.suggestedFix: No change needed. Optionally keep the statement as general advice and do not attribute it to the link.

issues.claim: Gregor Hohpe puts it this way: avoiding vendor lock-in has its own costs and creates its own lock-in, now to your in-house layer.
issues.problem: The excerpt supports only the general point that wrapping data access behind an abstraction layer may 'get you locked up into trying to escape from it'. The phrase 'lock-in to your in-house layer' is the author's own extension, presented as Hohpe's wording.
issues.suggestedFix: Soften the attribution: "Gregor Hohpe warns that avoiding lock-in has costs of its own and can trap you in the effort of escaping; here the new lock-in is to your own layer." Apply the same change in the ru block.
